clinicalPearls: Ophthalmia neonatorum is conjunctivitis in the first month of life, classically acquired as the infant passes through an infected birth canal
The two most important sexually transmitted causes are Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, alongside other bacteria, herpes simplex virus, and chemical irritation

Timing offers a clue: chemical conjunctivitis appears within the first day or two, gonococcal disease typically within the first few days, and chlamydial disease usually toward the end of the first week or later

Gonococcal ophthalmia is a sight-threatening emergency because it can rapidly cause corneal ulceration, perforation, and blindness, and it characteristically produces a hyperacute, profuse purulent discharge
Chlamydial ophthalmia is generally milder with mucopurulent discharge but is the commonest infective cause and can be accompanied by chlamydial pneumonitis
Diagnosis combines Gram stain and culture with nucleic acid amplification testing of conjunctival specimens to distinguish gonococcal, chlamydial, and other causes

Gonococcal disease requires systemic treatment with a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone plus saline irrigation, while chlamydial disease requires systemic macrolide therapy, as topical treatment alone is inadequate
Because it reflects maternal infection, management must include testing and treatment of the mother and her partners, and antenatal screening is the key preventive measure
reference.pathophysiology: Ophthalmia neonatorum arises when pathogens colonising the maternal genital tract contaminate the neonatal conjunctiva, most often during vaginal delivery, though ascending infection after membrane rupture can also occur. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is especially virulent: it can penetrate intact corneal epithelium, and its intense neutrophilic response with copious purulent exudate can rapidly progress to corneal ulceration and perforation. Chlamydia trachomatis, an obligate intracellular organism, infects conjunctival epithelial cells to produce a more subacute follicular or papillary conjunctivitis and may seed the nasopharynx and lungs, causing an afebrile pneumonitis. Chemical conjunctivitis, by contrast, is a transient self-limiting irritant reaction to topical prophylaxis rather than an infection.
additionalDifferentials: Other bacterial conjunctivitis (for example Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci, Gram-negative organisms)
Herpes simplex virus conjunctivitis or keratitis
Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction with secondary infection (dacryocystitis)
Congenital glaucoma presenting with tearing and a cloudy cornea
additionalInvestigations: Gram stain of conjunctival exudate looking for Gram-negative intracellular diplococci suggesting gonococcus
Bacterial culture of conjunctival swabs, including chocolate agar for Neisseria gonorrhoeae with antimicrobial susceptibility testing
Nucleic acid amplification testing for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Chlamydial-specific specimen collection sampling conjunctival cells for detection of the intracellular organism
Viral testing for herpes simplex when vesicles, keratitis, or systemic features are present
Maternal and partner screening for sexually transmitted infections to identify the source and guide treatment
redFlags: Hyperacute copious purulent discharge with marked lid oedema suggesting gonococcal infection
Corneal haze, ulceration, or clouding indicating sight-threatening keratitis
Systemic features such as poor feeding, lethargy, or respiratory signs suggesting disseminated gonococcal infection or chlamydial pneumonitis
Vesicular skin or eye lesions or encephalopathic features raising concern for neonatal herpes simplex
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition and appropriate systemic treatment the outlook is excellent, but delayed treatment of gonococcal ophthalmia can lead to corneal perforation and permanent blindness, and untreated chlamydial infection may be complicated by pneumonitis; antenatal screening and neonatal ocular prophylaxis have greatly reduced severe outcomes.
pitfalls: Attributing a purulent neonatal eye to harmless chemical or blocked-duct causes and missing gonococcal disease
Relying on topical antibiotics alone for gonococcal or chlamydial infection, which require systemic therapy
Failing to test for and treat coexisting infection (for example both gonorrhoea and chlamydia) and to consider chlamydial pneumonitis
Neglecting to investigate and treat the mother and her sexual partners
Overlooking herpes simplex, which needs antiviral rather than antibacterial treatment
references: BASHH UK national guidelines on the management of gonorrhoea and of chlamydial infection
CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines
Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Treat gonococcal ophthalmia urgently with a systemic third-generation cephalosporin (such as ceftriaxone or cefotaxime), as it is a sight-threatening emergency
Treat chlamydial ophthalmia with a systemic macrolide (oral erythromycin or azithromycin), which also covers concurrent chlamydial pneumonitis
Give systemic aciclovir when herpes simplex is implicated by vesicles or keratitis
Irrigate the eye with saline to clear the copious purulent discharge in gonococcal disease
Examine for and manage corneal involvement to prevent ulceration and perforation, with ophthalmology input
Treat the mother and her sexual partners for the identified sexually transmitted infection and screen accordingly
Reinforce neonatal ocular prophylaxis at birth as prevention
